title: Lightweight SDK request injector for non-blocking trace enrichment
creator: Aisha Kumar
description: Add a minimal-cost SDK-level hook that injects Redwood trace metadata and lightweight enrichment into outgoing requests without blocking the application thread. Goal is to provide consistent context propagation, optional baggage fields (customer_id/session_id), and a non-blocking path that defers expensive enrichments to a best-effort async writer. This enables downstream services and our tracing pipeline to reconstruct request graphs while keeping per-request latency overhead negligible.
acceptance_criteria: SDK hook exposes a single API: TraceInjector.inject(requestMetadata) usable from HTTP/gRPC/queue clients
P95 CPU overhead per-request attributable to injector < 0.5ms on benchmarked workloads
When enabled, headers x-redwood-trace or traceparent are injected consistently across sync/async clients
Optional baggage keys (configurable whitelist) are attached as structured headers and copied to logs via structured-log keys
If downstream rejects headers (size limits), injector falls back to trace id propagation only and records a metric
Instrumentation passes language SDK unit tests and interop tests against local trace bridge (simulated collector)
Feature gate exists: REDWOOD_SDK_TRACE_INJECTOR (env/config) and can be toggled without restart where supported
implementation_notes: Core path: synchronous header injection that writes a compact binary/hex trace id + sampling flag into x-redwood-trace header (14 bytes payload) to minimize serialization cost
Enrichment path: optional JSON payload (baggage) is written to an async ring-buffer and flushed by a background worker; if buffer full, drop with metric and move on
Language runtimes: implement in node/python/go/java SDKs with identical header schema and helper utilities to avoid per-language drift
Avoid allocations on hot path: pre-serialize constant header prefixes, reuse buffers from a thread-local pool
Compatibility: always include traceparent header for W3C compatibility and set x-redwood-trace as preferred; document precedence rules
Sampling: respect existing sampling decision in request context; if absent, call sampler once in injector and attach decision to header
Telemetry: emit metrics: injector.latency_ms P50/95/99, injector.dropped_enrichments_count, injector.fallback_count
Security: baggage whitelist must be enforced; sensitive keys should never be forwarded. Validate length and characters to prevent header-injection attacks
testing_plan: Unit tests for header serialization, sampling decisions, and baggage whitelist enforcement
Benchmarks: microbench harness to measure p50/p95 cost with 100k requests/sec synthetic driver
Integration tests: end-to-end with local trace collector ensuring spans link across services
Fault injection: simulate slow background worker, full ring buffer, and verify request tail latency unaffected
Compatibility matrix: verify with HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, gRPC, and our websocket proxy path
Load test: run against dedicated staging cluster replicating typical customer burst patterns to confirm <0.5ms p95 overhead
rollout_plan: Feature will be rolled out behind a global feature gate: start with internal apps (canary cohort) for 48 hours
Monitor injector.* metrics and trace link rate; if drops exceed threshold (>0.1% of requests), pause rollout
Expand to PLG customers in waves by account tier over 2 weeks, then to all hosted traffic
Provide quick rollback via feature gate and SDK config toggle; for older SDKs pre-release a compatibility shim
migration_strategy: Newer SDKs will enable injector off-by-default. For Dedicated/Private customers, provide an opt-in config and a migration patch that updates installed SDKs. Document headers and backward-compat behavior. Provide a small CLI check tool to validate downstream collectors accept x-redwood-trace and traceparent headers.
risks_mitigations: Risk: header size and customer proxies dropping/stripping headers -> Mitigation: keep x-redwood-trace compact and fallback to traceparent
Risk: sensitive data leakage via baggage -> Mitigation: enforce strict whitelist and static analysis lint rule in SDK builds
Risk: background worker CPU contention causing GC spikes -> Mitigation: bounded ring buffer, backpressure metrics and dropped-count alerts
Risk: cross-language drift causing link failures -> Mitigation: shared spec, interop tests as part of CI, and common serializer library where possible
